title: HeapWell Dedicated GPU intake — reserve, isolation, and surge playbook
summary: Initial discovery with HeapWell about moving inference to Redwood Dedicated. Focus on sizing reserved GPUs, tenant isolation, burst/warm pool strategy and fallback to hosted variants. Key ask: run a cost/latency pilot and share SOC2/KMS details.
next_steps: Redwood to send Dedicated pricing + burst pricing examples (Maya) by 2026-11-04
HeapWell to share representative traffic traces and 7-day peak window (Samir) by 2026-11-06
Schedule 2-hour benchmark with HeapWell model and token profile (Owen + Samir) week of 2026-11-09
Redwood to provide SOC2 + private deployment notes and KMS integration guide (Owen) by 2026-11-05
action_items: Maya Chen - Email Dedicated pricing PDF and two burst scenarios - 2026-11-04
Owen Patel - Prepare benchmark runbook and prewarm/warm-pool test configs - 2026-11-08
Samir Qureshi - Export 7 days of traffic histograms and token-per-request distribution - 2026-11-06
Liam Carter - Internal list of compliance owners and procurement timeline (ballpark) - 2026-11-06
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-02
Start: 14:00 PST
Duration: 44 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Owen Patel (Redwood SE), Liam Carter (CTO, HeapWell), Nina Rosario (Head of ML), Samir Qureshi (Infra Eng), Priya Das (Product)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Maya from Redwood, I run AE for the west region. With me is Owen, he's our infra/SE. Would you like to do quick intros?
[00:07] Liam Carter: Yeah hi, Liam, CTO at HeapWell, we build a document intelligence product for enterprise customers.
[00:10] Nina Rosario: Nina, Head of ML, mainly owning inference ops and model quality.
[00:14] Samir Qureshi: Samir, infra engineer, I manage our GPU fleet and cloud setup.
[00:18] Priya Das: Priya, product, focused on ML latency and customer SLAs.
[00:21] Owen Patel: Owen, Redwood SE. I'll run the benchmark/ops side of things.
[00:25] Maya Chen: Great. The goal today — understand your workload and see how Dedicated (reserved GPUs) fits, especially around isolation and your burst patterns.

[00:36] Priya Das: Quick framing — we currently run a mixed approach: some models on hosted endpoints and a small self-hosted cluster for heavier workloads. We're exploring Dedicated because of latency predictability and data isolation.
[00:47] Maya Chen: Got it. What are the main triggers for Dedicated vs staying hosted?
[00:51] Liam Carter: A few: regulatory customers asking for stronger isolation, predictable latency at scale, and cost predictability. Also our SSO/compliance asks — we need KMS for key material and audit logs retained longer.
[01:05] Samir Qureshi: And we hit big spikes — product launches cause 10x QPS for 10–20 minute windows. Our current autoscaling is slow and some requests time out.

[01:18] Owen Patel: Good to know. Can you walk through the traffic profile — baseline concurrency, typical tokens/request, and peak QPS?
[01:24] Samir Qureshi: Sure. Baseline is roughly 50 concurrent short chat requests, each ~60 tokens. Peak launches go to about 500 concurrent and token counts climb to 200 per request for long document summarization.
[01:38] Nina Rosario: Also note we have long-running rerank jobs (non-interactive) that we schedule, those prefer batch but sometimes collide with real-time traffic.

[01:50] Owen Patel: That's helpful. For Dedicated sizing we typically ask for 95th percentile concurrent and a token distribution. For a rough calc: 500 concurrent at 200 tokens — do you have desired P95 latency SLO?
[02:03] Priya Das: P95 under 300 ms for short chat, under 800 ms for long summarization would be great.
[02:09] Owen Patel: Okay. For those SLOs we can explore a combination: reserved GPU pool sized for baseline plus a warm prewarmed pool that covers bursts. Alternatively, reserved for baseline and bursts handled by burst capacity or failover to hosted — both have tradeoffs.

[02:24] Liam Carter: We want to avoid failure during launches. Basically minimal errors; we can accept slightly higher latency for a small percentage but not 50% errors.
[02:31] Maya Chen: Right — Redwood has a few strategies: 1) Keep warm prewarmed instances in Dedicated (costly but fastest), 2) Use burst to Hosted with automated model variant fallback (cheaper but network hop + possible data routing concerns), 3) Use a lower-cost quantized model variant in Dedicated as a graceful degradation.

[02:49] Nina Rosario: That quantized idea is interesting. We worry about quality drop though — we need A/B to ensure it's acceptable.
[02:55] Owen Patel: Totally. Part of Redwood Optimize is recommending which quantization/model variants hit cost/latency points with minimal quality regression. We can run evals on your prompt set.

[03:06] Samir Qureshi: On isolation — we need tenant isolation and per-customer encryption keys. Can Redwood Dedicated be VPC-only and integrate with our KMS?
[03:14] Maya Chen: Yes, Dedicated supports VPC-only private endpoints and integrates with customer KMS/HSM for model and data keys. We also provide audit logs and can push them to your logging endpoint.

[03:25] Priya Das: Retention requirements — we need 3 years of audit logs for certain customers. Is that standard?
[03:30] Owen Patel: We can provide long-term retention as an add-on; we typically ship logs to your S3/GCS with lifecycle rules. We'll include specifics in the SOC2/compliance docs.

[03:40] Liam Carter: On pricing — we need an example that shows cost for reserved GPUs sized for baseline, cost of keeping a warm prewarm pool for bursts, and cost of fallback to Hosted.
[03:48] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we'll send a few scenarios. Do you have any internal preference for preferred GPU type? A100s, H100s, or lower-spec?
[03:55] Samir Qureshi: We primarily use A100 today but are open to H100 if latency gains justify. Pricing is a big factor.

[04:04] Owen Patel: For H100 you typically see better perf on large-context models and for KV cache heavy workloads. For many chat workloads A100 is still very cost-effective. We'll include both profiles in the scenarios.

[04:18] Nina Rosario: How does Redwood handle model version pinning and rollouts in Dedicated? We want canary and fallback policies without manual infra changes.
[04:26] Maya Chen: The Console supports per-route/model rollouts — canary percentages, automatic fallback to a pinned variant if latency or error thresholds hit, and traffic split control. All declarative.

[04:36] Samir Qureshi: On burst capacity — is prewarming at the GPU container level or instance level? If we prewarm, how long to spin additional capacity?
[04:44] Owen Patel: Prewarming involves keeping model weights loaded on GPUs (warm containers). If we need to scale beyond warm pool, cold-start can take 30–120 seconds depending on model size and quantization. Hosted burst typically has similar cold-start unless a warm container exists there. Warm pools greatly reduce that time.

[04:59] Priya Das: So for 10–20 minute spikes, warm pool seems worth it. But cost wise we need a number.
[05:04] Maya Chen: We'll provide cost per idle-warm-GPU-hour vs cost per on-demand-burst minute. Also runbook recommendations like prewarming during known launch windows and auto-schedule.

[05:15] Liam Carter: What about multi-tenant isolation? We need hardware isolation for some regulated customers. Is that possible?
[05:20] Owen Patel: Dedicated supports node-level isolation — you can have single-tenant nodes pinned for a customer. That can be reserved capacity or we can configure anti-affinity. This is more expensive but it meets stricter compliance.

[05:33] Nina Rosario: And network egress — if we route bursts to Hosted, is any sensitive data leaving our VPC?
[05:38] Maya Chen: Good question. With VPC + private networking, Hosted bursts will require data egress through Redwood's control plane. For regulated data, we often recommend Dedicated-only bump or localizing burst to a dedicated edge region. We'll document the exact networking path.

[05:52] Samir Qureshi: For KMS keys, do you support bringing your own key material and HSM?
[05:56] Owen Patel: Yes BYOK with HSM integration — we support common KMS providers and rotate keys per your policy. We'll include the integration guide.

[06:05] Priya Das: Timeline — procurement is Q1 2027; we'd like a pilot in December to validate cost. Is that feasible?
[06:11] Maya Chen: Yes. A December pilot works. Next steps would be: you share traffic traces and preferred models, we scope a 1–2 week benchmark then run an isolated pilot with a small reserved pool + warm pool and provide results.

[06:24] Liam Carter: For the benchmark, we want end-to-end latency from our app through Redwood and back, with a token mix.
[06:29] Owen Patel: We'll provide a benchmark runbook and a test harness. Prefer to run your model artifacts in our Dedicated runtime if possible, or we can use equivalent open weights if licensed.

[06:40] Nina Rosario: Licensing — we have a proprietary finetuned LLM. How do we handle model artifacts? Can we bring model weights and keep them in our VPC?
[06:47] Owen Patel: For Private/Dedicated we support customer-managed model artifacts stored in your object store behind VPC. We can mount those for inference without copying to public storage.

[06:57] Priya Das: Security review will want a list of subprocessors and any partners.
[07:02] Maya Chen: We'll share a vendor list and SOC2 report. Also our Data Processing Addendum (DPA).

[07:08] Samir Qureshi: One technical detail — KV cache sharing across requests. We do interactive chat with long contexts — is the KV cache per-connection?
[07:15] Owen Patel: Yes per-session/KV cache is managed; we surface hooks for cache priming and eviction. Also we can tune chunk sizes for long-context docs.

[07:24] Liam Carter: Any limits on number of model variants pinned in Dedicated?
[07:28] Owen Patel: No hard limit; each variant has memory/slot cost. We recommend keeping common fallbacks and can automate auto-prune for stale variants.

[07:37] Maya Chen: Let's talk ops playbook for a launch spike. Typical playbooks include: pre-schedule prewarms, set canary traffic split to monitor errors, configure fallback quantized variant at N% traffic, and enable hosted-burst as last resort. Which of these do you want to prioritize?
[07:53] Priya Das: Prewarm + quantized fallback. Hosted as last resort but we'd prefer to avoid network leaving concerns.

[07:59] Samir Qureshi: We'll need automated instrumentation to flip the fallback quickly. Can the Console do that?
[08:03] Owen Patel: Yes, Console supports threshold-based automations — if error rate > X or latency > Y for Z seconds, it can shift traffic to fallback. We'll demo that in the benchmark.

[08:14] Nina Rosario: For monitoring, we need token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latencies in our monitoring stack. Do you export to Prometheus/Grafana?
[08:21] Maya Chen: We can push metrics to your Prometheus endpoint and provide dashboard templates. Cost breakdowns per-token come through in the Console and via API export.

[08:32] Liam Carter: Procurement question — what's the commitment length for dedicated reserved pools?
[08:36] Maya Chen: We offer flexible terms: monthly reserved, 6/12 month committed, with pricing discounts for longer commitments. We can also do pilot credits for initial validation.

[08:45] Samir Qureshi: How do rolling upgrades and kernel selection happen? We can't have noisy upgrades mid-launch.
[08:51] Owen Patel: Rolling upgrades are scheduled and can be disabled during blackout windows. Kernel selection for inference runtime is tested on a canary subset before rolling wide. We respect maintenance windows you configure.

[08:59] Priya Das: SLOs — do you provide uptime/latency SLAs for Dedicated?
[09:04] Maya Chen: Yes Dedicated comes with SLA options — uptime and P99 latency objectives can be contracted; we can include those in SOW.

[09:12] Maya Chen: Any final constraints we haven't discussed?
[09:15] Liam Carter: Data residency for EU customers; some customers require EU-only processing. We have customers in EU.
[09:20] Owen Patel: We can map Dedicated pools to specific regions. For EU-only, we'd pin capacity in an EU region and ensure routing policies respect residency.

[09:30] Nina Rosario: One edge case — offline batch rerank jobs that saturate GPUs for hours; we want to protect real-time traffic. Does Redwood support priority scheduling?
[09:38] Owen Patel: Yes, priority queues and preemption policies are supported. You can configure compute weights and eviction thresholds so interactive traffic gets priority over batch.

[09:47] Samir Qureshi: That's good. For the pilot in December, we want two scenarios: 1) normal day baseline with small prewarm pool, 2) simulated launch spike with 10x concurrency. Can Redwood simulate that on Dedicated?
[09:59] Owen Patel: Yes we can orchestrate load tests against the Dedicated environment and measure end-to-end. We'll bring scripts and run them with your traces.

[10:10] Priya Das: About costs, we want a model of dollars per 1M tokens at baseline and under burst.
[10:15] Maya Chen: We'll produce a cost model with token assumptions and hourly prewarm cost.

[10:20] Liam Carter: When will you send pricing and the benchmark runbook?
[10:23] Maya Chen: We'll send pricing and two scenario examples by Wednesday 2026-11-04 and the runbook + SOC2 docs by Thursday 2026-11-05.

[10:31] Nina Rosario: Great. Anything else on security?
[10:33] Owen Patel: We'll include data flow diagrams and KMS integration steps.

[10:38] Maya Chen: Quick recap of next steps then: Redwood sends pricing, bench runbook, SOC2 + KMS guide; HeapWell sends traffic traces and a list of models/weights and procurement timeline. We'll schedule the benchmark week of 2026-11-09.

[10:55] Liam Carter: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[11:00] Maya Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with the artifacts.

End of transcript.
